title: ‘Elsinore’ Revisits Daniel Day-Lewis’ Infamous Walk-Off During ’80s ‘Hamlet’ Production
description: Audiences got the first glimpse at a triumphant and career-defining performance from Andrew Scott in “Elsinore” this weekend, but the Telluride play
body:
Audiences got the first glimpse at a triumphant and career-defining performance from Andrew Scott in “Elsinore” this weekend, but the Telluride player also delivers another important gift: legendary show business gossip.

	Central to the plot is an infamous real-life moment in the history of the U.K. theater — when Daniel Day-Lewis stopped cold during a performance of “Hamlet,” before stalking off stage and never coming back. Ever.
	

	“Elsinore” opens in 1989, during a production of “Hamlet” at London’s National Theater. During a fraught encounter between Hamlet and the ghost of his father, an actor freezes before exiting entirely. The incident shocks audience members and sends cast and crew into a meltdown.


	“That’s not supposed to happen,” deadpans a sassy house manager, watching the disaster unfold in real time on CCTV. Director Simon Stone’s camera follows the actor as he storms to his dressing room, where a slammed door reveals Day-Lewis’ name on a placard. The Telluride crowd erupted in laughter and surprise at the reveal. It reminded (or informed) them that it happened in the first place.

	“Elsinore” is the heart-wrenching true story of Scottish actor Ian Charelson. The star of “Chariots of Fire” had the chance of a lifetime to replace Day-Lewis as Hamlet in that same production, all while succumbing to complications from end-stage AIDS. He died 7 weeks after bowing out to rave reviews. Filmmakers and producers on “Elsinore” approached the matter sensitively, numerous sources told Variety, and screened a rough cut of the film for Day-Lewis’ reps before the Telluride premiere to get their blessing.
	

	So what happened on that fateful November day in 1989? Actors, academics and press are still trying to solve the puzzle 37 years later. The British media devoured the story, as even then Day-Lewis was synonymous with intense devotion to his craft. Urban legend goes that Day-Lewis saw the ghost of his own late father, the poet Cecil Day-Lewis, that night on stage. In 2012, the “Lincoln” star debunked this myth (though he gave quotes at the time that supported the supernatural anecdote). 

	That year was incredibly fraught for Day-Lewis. He’d wrapped production on “My Left Foot” and was barreling toward his first ever Academy Award, one he’d win four months later at the Dorothy Chandler Pavillion in 1990. The same year as the “Hamlet” debacle, he’d also met French actress Isabelle Adjani, with who he reportedly had a tumultuous relationship before a breakup in 1996.

	“I work in a certain way, and I never really felt the need to explain it or apologize for it, but in England, they thought I was unhinged,” Day-Lewis told Time magazine in 2012. “The press goes after you, and they don’t tend to let go.”

	On the ground in Telluride, we caught up with “Elsinore” producer Gabrielle Tana, who says the moment ultimately reinforces Charelson’s destiny.

	 “It was the dream come true. It was carpe diem, and he got an opportunity to do the thing that he always wanted to do,. Ian felt he was washed up, and all of a sudden this gift was there for him,” said Tana.

	Focus Features will release “Elsinore” in theaters on Nov. 20.

title: ‘The Debut’ Explodes at Telluride With Julianne Moore’s Gonzo, Career-Best Turn, Thanks to a Toolbelt, Unlit Cigarettes and a Faux Musical

body:
Jesse Eisenberg has made his most significant debut to date.

	There is a delicious irony at the center of “The Debut,” Eisenberg’s third feature as a director, which world premiered at the Telluride Film Festival: it is a film about a nobody who attacks a bit part as if it were the role of a lifetime — and it arrives as one of the fall’s genuine best picture contenders, ready to make Oscar darlings out of Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti.
	

	Rebecca Keagan of NBC News moderated the Q&A with Eisenberg, Moore and Giamatti. It was Giamatti’s first time seeing the film.


	Call it Eisenberg’s “Black Swan” by way of “Whiplash” and “Waiting for Guffman,” the whole fever dream staged inside a faux musical and relocated to a New Jersey rec center. Moore plays Mona Friedman, a meek housewife who hasn’t sung in front of anyone since church choir and is unexpectedly cast in a community-theater production — then transforms into a zealous method actor willing to wage war over a marginal role. Giamatti is Jerry, the tyrannical director billed, without irony, as the biggest name in New Jersey community theater. It is funny, then feral, then unexpectedly moving and it confirms that the filmmaker who won Kieran Culkin an Oscar with “A Real Pain” knows exactly how to build a showcase around actors.

	A24 sets it for Dec. 11, a release date that signals a studio going long — and A24 knows this walk. Twice it has turned an unlikely film into a best picture champion: “Moonlight,” which stunned the favored “La La Land and “Everything Everywhere All at Once,” an absurdist multiverse comedy that had no business winning and won anyway. “The Debut” hands the studio a broad, playable contender with two of the most beloved actors alive at its center.
	

	Start with Moore, who has quietly become the film’s frontrunner-in-waiting. She is a five-time nominee with a single win — “Still Alice,” more than a decade ago — and Mona is the sort of tragicomic tour de force that reintroduces a great actor to voters who may have forgotten how much they owe her. She plays it balls to the wall, fearless in the way of Natalie Portman or Cate Blanchett at full tilt. On Telluride’s Saturday afternoon screening, she drew spontaneous applause in the middle of two separate scenes — the kind of response that tells you everything.

	A sixth nomination is automatic. The win is the question, and the recent past is on her side: the modern Academy has grown notably comfortable handing out second — and even third — acting Oscars. Anthony Hopkins for “The Father,” Emma Stone for “Poor Things” (Stone, tellingly, produces “The Debut”), with Frances McDormand and Sean Penn all tripling up in recent years. A second Moore statuette would surprise no one.

	Giamatti’s case is different, and in some ways sweeter, because he is chasing his first. One of the most admired actors of his generation has never won — the “Sideways” snub remains a scar on the branch’s record, and his leading turn in “The Holdovers” lost to the “Oppenheimer” juggernaut. As Jerry, he has the flashier, more quotable role: the monstrous mentor, the archetype that won J.K. Simmons an Oscar in “Whiplash” but with heart. He also gets what may be the film’s best line — “That’s where everyone wants to be … center stage.” His likeliest and most winnable lane is supporting, the very category Culkin swept for Eisenberg two years ago. Lightning tends to strike the same script twice.

	There is something lovely, too, in the pairing of this and “Elsinore” on the same mountain: the two biggest swings at Telluride this year are both love letters to acting itself.

	“The Debut” is less a musical than a savage comedy about one — a movie set in the world of an original show rather than a wall-to-wall songbook. That distinction matters.

	Drew Daniels, fresh off “Anora,” shoots it; Emil Mosseri, an Oscar nominee for “Minari,” scores it; Bernadette Peters and Halle Bailey enrich an ensemble with real Broadway bona fides. Eisenberg, himself a screenplay nominee for “A Real Pain,” has written another original that plays far bigger than its logline. It has the bones of a lighthearted Tarantino picture spliced with the DNA of “Stranger Than Fiction” — and it arrived at Telluride with a résumé, then left with a possible frontrunner status.
	

	There are no small parts, the old theater adage goes, only small actors. “The Debut” turns the cliché into a thesis and dares you to disagree. Your move, Academy.

title: Original ‘Practical Magic’ Star Alexandra Artrip Addresses ‘Negativity’ Over Recasting in Sequel: They ‘Did What They Thought Was Best to Be Successful’
description: Alexandra Artrip, who played the youngest daughter of Sandra Bullock’s character Sally Owens in 1998’s “Practical Magic,” has weighed in on the sequ
body:
Alexandra Artrip, who played the youngest daughter of Sandra Bullock’s character Sally Owens in 1998’s “Practical Magic,” has weighed in on the sequel’s decision to recast her and fellow original actor Evan Rachel Wood in the upcoming sequel.

	Artrip played Antonia Owens alongside Wood as her older sister Kylie, but their roles were given to younger actresses Maisie Williams and Joey King, respectively, in “Practical Magic 2.” Wood spoke out about the recasting earlier in the week, saying that “no one who worked on the original movie” reached out to her. She said that she did hear from King, who took over her role as Kylie, and that she was a “sweetheart.” Artrip posted a video on Instagram and responded to comments criticizing the recastings.
	

	“I love hearing your stories and connections to the film, but I get comments like this a lot, and I see them going on a lot of content around the sequel,” Artrip said. “I think the sentiment is right, people are trying to show support for Evan and myself and the original film and everything it’s meant to so many people, but I just don’t want my stuff to be a space for negativity. Maisie and Joey are lovely actresses, and I’m sure the production team did what they thought was best for the film to be successful.”


	She added, “I just think we should support the film, give it a shot, go in with an open mind. Nothing can take away from what the original film was, and I’m excited that we’re able to build on that world with a new novel, new content in 2026, and that it’s given me a space to revisit all those beloved memories all these years later.”
	

	“Practical Magic 2” director Susanne Bier also weighed in on the recastings, telling Variety at the premiere that it was “not personal.”

	“The kids in the story are right out of college, so it wasn’t really a question,” she said. “We had to recast and we had to get some kids that [had been out of college].”

	“Practical Magic 2” opens in theaters on Sept. 10.

title: ‘Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger’ Review: An Uncharacteristically Polite and Sentimental Portrait of a Raucous Band and Phenomenon

body:
The 2016 documentary “Supersonic,” focused on Oasis’ beginnings and incredibly fast rise to superstardom, made no mention of what was then the most salient fact about the Gallagher brothers: that from 2009, they were no longer on speaking terms. Ten years after that Asif Kapadia-produced doc, the concert film “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger” — world premiering at the Venice Film Festival —begins by placing the split front and center. After a short montage, which includes actual footage of the infamous Rock en Seine gig where the brothers never even made it to the stage, the film takes us right into the rehearsal room where, in the summer of 2025, the newly reunited band is set to practice together for six weeks. The question of whether sparks will fly between the siblings within this confined space hangs heavily in the air, and nifty editing plays up the anxiety around the project. 
	

	But while some tension is palpable, sparks do not fly — or at least, filmmakers Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace  (whose previous rock docs include 2010’s Grammy-nominated “No Distance Left to Run,” about Oasis’ old ’90s rivals Blur) do not choose to show them if they do. It is soon clear that “Don’t Look Back in Anger” is far from an unvarnished portrait of an often fraught relationship, let alone a tabloid-style collection of shocking anecdotes. 


	Although neither Noel nor Liam can help expressing themselves, in new on-camera interviews, in the candid manner that they always have, they remain not just on their best behavior, but also at what feels like a PR-trained remove. Their professional focus — the usually raucous Liam is described by a band member as being uncharacteristically “business” in rehearsals — is in step with a film whose attempts to conceal its obvious financial raison d’etre often feel absurd and tacked-on.
	

	With the two brothers on somewhat guarded form, offering little insight into their own thoughts or emotions throughout this experience, the film dedicates a significant portion of its two-hour runtime to the fans. “Don’t Look Back in Anger” might have benefited from the hindsight of a few more years and constructed a compelling argument about what Oasis meant in 2025, especially in the U.K. The tour seemed the latest and most spectacular sign of a society-wide nostalgia for the 1990s, responding perhaps to a series of national disasters (Brexit, Covid-19, rapidly succeeding prime ministers), and occurring in the middle of a wave of national pride and hope (the soccer) that was itself shoring up against decidedly less positive attitudes (the rise of right-wing politicians and policies). 

	All this, compared to what Oasis meant at its peak in 1996, would make for a fascinating film that could also enshrine the band’s significance more successfully than yet another montage of newspaper headlines or references to album sales. As it is, the film only briefly and somewhat ironically touches on those world events that might explain why the 2025 tour was such a phenomenon. Over a rapid-fire montage showing footage of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, Keir Starmer, online videos of robots falling over, and other more-or-less severe indignities, Liam declares, “When Oasis split up, everything went to shit.” He continues, “People, more than ever now, they want to escape.” 

	This idea that Oasis’s music provides a form of escape or release is entirely supported by the plentiful footage of concert-goers included in the film. Shouting out the lyrics like their lives depend on it, clutching at their loved ones, crying, even praying, and often in a state of apparent inebriation, these men and women are a far cry from the dreaded, zombie-like GenZ crowds that have frustrated countless acts in recent years — even though most of the fans seen in the film are under 30. 

	This enthusiasm could be partly explained by the band’s unexpected reunion, but brief inserts of footage from Oasis’ triumphant shows at Knebworth in 1996 suggest that the Mancunian band engenders a type of fandom of a particularly feverish kind. The film puts it plainly in a sequence showing police security gathered ahead of the first reunion gig, as the chief of police tells the others that fans are expected to have “a herd mentality similar to that of football crowds.” 
	

	It seems an odd choice, then, for the film to go in a less visceral and more sentimental direction. The impressive concert footage and appropriately very loud sound design (by “The Zone of Interest” Oscar winner Tarn Willers and James Mather) showcases big chunks of songs at their best, but they are frequently interrupted either by platitudes from the brothers which fans have surely heard before, or by brief tangents centered on fans from around the world. A woman in Brazil has named her dog after guitarist Paul “Bonehead” Arthurs; two female divers in South Korea talk about their friendship and the song “Acquiesce.” 

	The most awkward if well-meaning inclusion is a survivor of the 2017 Manchester Arena attack which took place during an Ariana Grande concert. The young girl describes struggling with survivor’s guilt at the time, and finding solace in hearing Noel’s iconic ballad “Don’t Look Back in Anger” at a vigil; she is later seen singing along to the song at one of the reunion shows. Such attempts to touch on the highly personal connections people have to Oasis’s music feel clumsy and forced, especially when juxtaposed with the brothers’ rather anonymous comments.

	The film’s generally po-faced attitude as a whole seems an odd fit for the Gallaghers. It is difficult to imagine them not responding with a barb of some kind to the footage of an actual sermon. The priest likens the concert crowds to a pilgrimage, and quotes Matthew 18:21 (“Lord, how many times must I forgive my brother?”) before claiming that the people have come not so much for the music as “for the reconciliation between two brothers.” The somewhat bombastic approach of screenwriter and “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight, who created and wrote the doc, has been successful elsewhere, but feels at odds with the band’s ethos here. 

	These stabs at earnestness do nothing to diminish the feeling of the concert film being little more than a cash grab. Likewise, the repeated point about Oasis’ working-class origins, while true, comes across as another attempt at striking a sentimental chord — in a way that feels anathema to Oasis. In a context where the price of concert tickets today excludes working-class fans from attending shows at all, it feels doubly insincere. 
	

	It did not have to be this way. In one throwaway moment in the film, as Liam asks audiences to turn around and lock arms with the people around them, he refers to the people in the cheap seats, before adding, “Actually there are no cheap seats, sorry about that.” No Oasis fan would reproach the band for making a lot of money on their tour; in fact, there is no doubt that they would have cherished the chance to hear the two brothers bragging again together about how rich and successful they are, just like they used to do. “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger” should be of interest to fans who missed the 2025 tour or are seeking to relive some of its emotion. But its polite treatment of such a momentous event strips it of some of the specificity and intensity that are no doubt behind the band’s continued popularity.

title: Three Films, and a Second Oscar? How Penélope Cruz Could Dominate Awards Season With ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘The Invite’ and ‘Bunker’
description:
Penélope Cruz became an Oscar winner when 2008’s “Vicky Cristina Barcelona” made her the first Spanish actress to win an acting Oscar.

	Seventeen y
body:
Penélope Cruz became an Oscar winner when 2008’s “Vicky Cristina Barcelona” made her the first Spanish actress to win an acting Oscar.

	Seventeen years later, she is not chasing a second statuette so much as choosing which vehicle to ride to the ceremony — because this season she has three.

	The biggest of the three isn’t even her largest role. 


	Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra” — the Federico García Lorca-inspired epic that shared the best director prize at Cannes, drew a near-record ovation on the Croisette and sold to Netflix in a bidding war — is shaping up as the streamer’s marquee awards title of the year. Cruz surfaces in it as a bawdy cabaret singer, a role the size of a cameo that critics off the Croisette and now here at Telluride have already tagged a scene-stealer.
	

	In Olivia Wilde’s A24 dinner-party comedy “The Invite,” which opened over the summer, she has another scene-stealing part opposite Edward Norton, a second potential route into the supporting actress race.

	And then there is “Bunker,” Florian Zeller’s follow-through on the promise of “The Father,” which bows in Venice competition Sept. 8. Zeller wrote it for Cruz and her real-life husband Javier Bardem — their eighth film together — and built it around a marriage of 17 years, roughly the length of their own. Cruz plays the wife whose disillusionment becomes the story’s emotional core, opposite Bardem as an architect drawn into building a survivalist bunker for a reclusive tech billionaire. Sony Pictures Classics, which turned “The Father” into a six-nomination contender that won two — best actor for Anthony Hopkins and adapted screenplay for Zeller himself — is lining up a lead actress run after Venice and Toronto, and even betting Bardem can land in best actor beside her, making “Bunker” a two-front campaign before Cruz’s other films enter the frame.
	

	The genuinely unprecedented possibility is what happens if both supporting turns (and lead) catch fire — because this is the first season it even could.



	

					Penelope Cruz in “La Bola Negra”
									Cannes
	



	Earlier this year, the Academy rewrote one of its oldest acting rules. Beginning with this year’s 99th Academy Awards, a performer can land two nominations in the same category, provided both performances finish among the top five in nominations voting. For decades, the lower vote-getter was simply erased. Now both can stand. Cruz is the marquee test case — Variety war-gamed this exact scenario when the rule changed.

	It helps that all three films are already mounting serious campaigns of their own, quite apart from Cruz — buzz she can borrow without having to manufacture it, and dip into when she feels like it, not because she has to.

	But it can also set a trap. The same rule that makes a double nom possible makes vote splitting potentially fatal for a campaign. If Cruz’s support scatters across two films, neither performance may crack the top five and if concentrated on one, she could be deemed far safer. However, push too hard on both and she risks walking away with nothing, where a single campaign would have guaranteed her a seat.

	The burden falls on three distributors, not one. 

	Sony Pictures Classics will carry the lead in “Bunker”; Netflix and A24 hold the supporting hopefuls, each with every incentive to protect its own contender rather than share the road. They can coordinate in ways that serve Cruz — or quietly compete for the same Oscar oxygen.

	For Cruz, the best case is that the films read as complementary rather than rivalry.

	Netflix is not treating its one like a cameo showcase. The company has handed “La Bola Negra” the longest exclusive theatrical window in its history — 47 days in theaters from Oct. 16 before it streams Dec. 2, past even the run it once gave “Marriage Story” — the surest tell that it intends a full best picture campaign, not a token qualifying run. It is likely Netflix’s spearhead this year, as the Cannes conqueror the awards team has been waiting for and that is the muscle that can uplift even a supporting cameo into the race. It doesn’t hurt that Toronto is handing Cruz a Special Tribute Award as the film makes its North American rounds, another plank in a recognition narrative Netflix is glad to build upon.
	

	There is a bigger story underneath, too. “La Bola Negra” is a Spanish-language epic Netflix is pushing to the front of the field and Cruz has long been the international face Academy voters know best, and this season she sits at the center of a Spanish-language surge pressing into the awards conversation on its own terms as a cultural dimension her résumé alone never carried.

	And then we have the question about the second Oscar itself.

	Cruz has already done what most actors spend a career chasing when she won the Oscar in 2009. However, there was a bit of an asterisk many felt since Kate Winslet, who had swept the circuit for “The Reader,” was shockingly moved to lead by the Academy where she ultimately won. Wouldn’t it be great to do a proper seasonal long coronation on one of the most astounding and talented international performers? A second win would place her in the small circle of performers with multiple acting Oscars in supporting actress. Only two — Dianne Wiest (“Hannah and Her Sisters” and “Bullets Over Broadway”) and Shelley Winters (“The Diary of Anne Frank” and “A Patch of Blue”).

	But the most interesting story may be the simplest. Cruz has spent a career refusing to be any one thing in the movies. And now, she is refusing to be in any one category.

title: Hey, Oscars: No Sympathy Required to Give Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ the Consideration It Deserves
description:
Let’s dispense with the suspense. Mike Leigh has been nominated for an Academy Award seven times and has won it zero times. That seems wrong.

	He h
body:
Let’s dispense with the suspense. Mike Leigh has been nominated for an Academy Award seven times and has won it zero times. That seems wrong.

	He has a Palme d’Or, a Golden Lion, five decades of films that taught generations of actors what unglamorous truth looks like and one of the most distinctive bodies of work in modern British cinema. What he does not have is an Oscar — and based on the reviews and reactions out of the Telluride Film Festival, where the film bowed Friday night, it’s about damn time he got one.
	

	“Tender Loving Care” arrives carrying the weight none of Leigh’s previous films did. At 83, and contending with myosotis, a muscle-wasting condition that kept him from his own Telluride premiere, Leigh has said this is most likely his last film. Bleecker Street opens it Dec. 4 after a fall festival run the industry reserves for titles it takes seriously.


	That makes the season’s obvious question unavoidable: What should the Academy do with Mike Leigh’s final film? The answer is not — give him an Oscar because he is 83.

	It is — watch the movie, and you’ll see why you’d want to.

	“Tender Loving Care” does not need a sympathy campaign. It is vintage Leigh — wry, melancholy, humane, alert to the small emotional humiliations that become, over the course of a life, the events that define us. Kate O’Flynn’s Amy anchors it — an Emmy nominee for “Widow’s Bay,” and when the trophies are handed out Sept. 14, very possibly a winner — a social worker steadying a father in decline, gutted by a breakup and kept upright by wine and by Rosie, the live-wire best friend played exquisitely by Alice Bailey Johnson. Marion Bailey, as Amy’s mother, has already emerged from Telluride as a standout, a veteran thespian never given her proper due. 
	

	A film about the daily labor of caring for people, made by a filmmaker who has spent 50 years caring, without vanity, about the interior lives most movies never bother to notice. It’s a perfect bookend to a career — and it closes on perhaps the most haunting final shot of any film in a decade. There’s a smaller bookend folded inside it, too: Leigh gave O’Flynn her first job, on “Happy-Go-Lucky,” at 21. She returns for his last.

	That sets up a campaign with an unusual shape and real vigor. Leigh carries the legacy narrative, but the film has to prove first that the work is competitive in a year crowded with filmmakers nursing overdue stories of their own.

	So the cleanest argument for Leigh is historical, not sentimental.

	Seven nominations and zero wins is a remarkable record. Twice — for “Secrets & Lies” and “Vera Drake” — the Academy nominated Leigh for both writing and directing in the same year, the dual embrace it reserves for its favorites. It has honored him again and again without ever closing the final distance. This is not an artist who spent a career waiting for his first invitation.

	The performances could help carry him there. O’Flynn and Bailey have the most obvious pathways, though where their teams ultimately campaign is still being sorted — and pundits will argue over where the two should land, which is rarely where they actually do.



	

					Kate O’Flynn, Paul Jesson and Marion Bailey in “Tender Loving Care”
									Thin Man Films Ltd and Bleecker Street
	



	When two women read as co-leads, the Academy has grown allergic to rewarding both in the same category: the last time it nominated two lead actresses from a single film was “Thelma & Louise,” Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis, in 1991. So I’d bet the campaign splits them — O’Flynn, the anchor, in lead actress and Bailey in supporting.

	It should be duly noted, Bailey Johnson would be a worthy option to join whichever lady decides on the supporting campaign and as the ailing father, Paul Jesson is also incredibly rich and dynamic and would be worthy of consideration.

	But Bleecker Street will have to decide where to spend. An intimate British drama cannot campaign on every front with the force of a studio tent-pole.

	That is where the festival strategy matters. Telluride built the word-of-mouth. Toronto should widen the critical and industry conversation. The New York Film Festival drops the film into the center of the American awards ecosystem. The distributor’s job now is turning that accumulation into industry votes.
	

	There is a trap in the “last film” framing, too. Leigh’s age and health explain the stakes of the moment, but they should never become the reason to vote. The Academy has a long, familiar habit of honoring artists after the fact. The more respectful campaign makes the case while the artist is still here — still working at full command of his gifts.

	This is not a plea for a career-achievement handout. It is simply an argument that the film should earn the consideration on its own merits, and that a body claiming to honor the year’s best would embarrass itself to overlook a master telling us, gently, that he is done.

	He named the film “Tender Loving Care.” The least the Academy can do is extend some.

title: Liam and Noel Gallagher Raise Fists and Electrify Venice as Oasis Doc Gets 8-Minute Standing Ovation
description: Oasis mania hit Venice Film Festival on Saturday night as Liam and Noel Gallagher presented the world premiere of their highly anticipated documenta
body:
Oasis mania hit Venice Film Festival on Saturday night as Liam and Noel Gallagher presented the world premiere of their highly anticipated documentary “Don’t Look Back in Anger.”

	The rock doc received an eight-minute standing ovation as the once-estranged brothers held hands and raised them triumphantly. Though the Gallaghers aren’t one for emotions, Noel at one point appeared to be wiping tears from his eyes while Liam hyped up the crowd. The atmosphere inside the Palazzo del Cinema was electric, with fans clamoring to get a photo, autograph or just a look at the iconic musicians. Before the screening, the brothers were greeted with cheers of “C’mon, boys!” and “Fight!” One fan even brought a Manchester City flag (their football club of choice) and flew it over the balcony.
	

	As the documentary rolled on, the rowdiness continued — attendees clapped after most of the live performances in the film and, as the audience sang along to “Champagne Supernova,” several were reduced to audible tears. During the actual standing ovation, the brothers — understandably new to the film festival world — looked like they had no idea what to do, with Liam eyeing his watch and mouthing, “Should we fuck off?” before creator Steven Knight seemingly convinced him to stay. But all hell broke loose when the Gallaghers descended into the crowd to sign autographs, turning the theater into a mild mosh pit as fans jockeyed for a selfie or signature. One thing’s for sure, this is likely to be the closest Venice Film Festival gets to a rock concert.


	Earlier on the red carpet, Italian fans donned their best bucket hats and band merch, singing along to “Acquiesece” and “Wonderwall” as they waited for Liam and Noel to arrive. Ever the rock ‘n’ roll stars, when they finally did, it was through the cinema’s entrance instead of from a car at the start of the carpet, causing screams to erupt. The Gallaghers, known for their love of windbreakers and Fred Perry polos, dressed smartly for the occasion in all black (though still decidedly unfancy, with Liam layering a T-shirt underneath a blazer and Noel wearing a zip-up jacket). Fans chanted “Oasis! Oasis! Oasis!” as the brothers signed autographs separately, before coming together to pose for photos — even holding hands and raising them up victoriously for one shot.
	

	Directed by Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace, the documentary “charts Liam and Noel Gallagher’s triumphant reunion tour, Oasis Live ‘25, one of the most anticipated rock ‘n’ roll comebacks of our time,” according to its official synopsis. The film, which premieres in theaters Sept. 11 before bowing on Disney+ later this year, boasts footage of the band both backstage and onstage as well as the first joint interview with often-feuding brothers Noel and Liam in over 20 years. 

	The Oasis reunion tour last year marked the first time the Gallagher brothers had played together since 2009. Tickets for the tour sold out immediately and it went on to generate hundreds of millions of dollars across dates in the U.K., North America, South Korea, Japan, Australia, Argentina, Chile and Brazil.

	The success of Oasis Live ’25 — and the fact that the brothers are still getting along well enough to do press for their documentary together — has sparked rumors of a further Oasis tour, perhaps next year. Though the Gallaghers weren’t on hand at the film’s press conference earlier on Saturday to field questions, the band has posted several cryptic teasers on Instagram that have sent fans into detective mode. Adding to the speculation, Noel said in a recent interview on Talksport: “Let’s put it this way: there’s no football tournament on next year, so we’ve got to do something in the summer, right?”

title: ‘Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes’ Review: The Legendary Rocker Gets a Lively Doc That Asks: Who Are You? And Then Doesn’t Fully Answer It
description: Every rock god has his ultimate gesture of power, and for Pete Townshend it was not the way he liked to smash his guitar (though that came close). N
body:
Every rock god has his ultimate gesture of power, and for Pete Townshend it was not the way he liked to smash his guitar (though that came close). No, the quintessential Townshend power sign was his giant circular windmill strum, arm outstretched and twirling, gathering centrifugal force to slam that pick up through the guitar strings, creating the loudest chord humanly possible.

	The impulse behind that gesture — the destructive fury of it ­— is the same one that gave rise to Led Zeppelin and punk. And you get to see Townshend do it a bunch of times in Frank Marshall and Nigel Sinclair’s “Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes,” the lively and somewhat scattered documentary that just premiered at Telluride. As music docs go, it’s a serviceable rock ride, with plenty of great archival footage that’s never been seen before. (It’s been culled from long-lost 16mm reels shot at Holmhurst Manor in 1972, as well as Townshend’s home movies and outtakes from the Who’s 1970 Isle of Wight performance.)
	

	But the power-chord side of Townshend ends up taking something of a back seat in “Behind Blue Eyes.” The movie is more interested in his anguished moody poetic side, the one that created the great rock opera “Tommy” (a work nearly as pivotal as “Sgt. Pepper,” and one built around Townshend’s childhood trauma), as well as his desire to expand beyond it by making rock over into something bigger, bolder, more confessionally grandiose.


	Townshend was a Mod who grew up into a rock intellectual who still talked like a bloke. He’s incredibly thoughtful, and always has been, but he could also be something of a doomy drama queen. He led the early Who with burn-it-all-down ferocity, yet was always concerned about the effects of rock, wanting it to stay positive. The film sketches in how Townshend got his start in art school, and in his case it really stuck. He wanted rock to be an art form. He swiped the idea of guitar-smashing from films he was shown as a student of avant-garde classical musicians destroying pianos. His days with the Who began as a lark (he never planned to make a career of it), but the group became a draw in West London. There’s a great clip of them from 1965 playing “I Can’t Explain,” with its tight chords that were so ’50s yet so new, as Townshend bops out to it. 
	

	It’s strange, though, that “Behind Blue Eyes” skips over the epochal moment of “My Generation,” one of the 10 most seismic and influential songs in the history of rock ‘n’ roll. When punk finally came along, the movie talks about how Townshend, who totally dug the punk scene, tried to cozy up to Johnny Rotten and got nowhere. It notes how much influence the Who had on punk — but that would be “My Generation,” which the film never got around to mentioning!

	Other jarring omissions: We’re informed that Keith Moon, the Who’s thrash genius of a drummer, died of a drug overdose (the drug was chlomethiazole, a sedative prescribed to alleviate the symptoms of alcohol withdrawal), but the movie never says a word about his drinking. (He might have been the biggest drinker in the history of rock.) And while we’re told that Townshend was dead set against making a movie of “Tommy,” the film leaves out the impact of Ken Russell’s opulently feverish 1975 big-screen version.

	There’s already a definitive movie about the Who, the formative rock doc “The Kids Are Alright” (1979), so Marshall and Sinclair may have felt that they could sort of skip through the band’s career. Yet “Behind Blue Eyes,” though it is a film about Townshend, remains very, very Who centered. Townshend, who’s 81 now, sits for an extended interview, wearing a red wool cap over his bald head. He is open and circumspect, with a disarming gentleness. He tells the Who’s story — as does Roger Daltrey, who sat down for the filmmakers — with a ripe feeling for the heights they scaled and a wistful sense of how far away the feuds and valleys now seem.

	“Behind Blue Eyes” opens, quite dramatically, on the crisis Townshend was going through after “Tommy” became a majestic success. Townshend had evolved his whole idea for a rock opera out of the two years, starting at age four, when he was abandoned by his parents and sent to live with his sexually debauched grandmother. He was never abused, but he says he was so distraught that he literally tuned out reality; he became that “deaf, dumb and blind kid.” Townshend composed and recorded the music for “Tommy” at home (in demos that were then built on in the studio). The band, at that point, had become entirely his. (He says the other three band members just wanted to party and sleep around.) But once “Tommy” changed the game for the Who, how could they top it? In films from the time, we see the fear frozen onto Townshend’s face.
	

	The Holmhurst Manor footage shows the members of the Who sitting around the Jacobean country house in East Sussex that was purchased by Roger Daltrey in 1970 (it was one of those aristocratic estates that noise-making British bands of the ’70s loved to record in), hashing out where they were going to go next. Because they had no idea. And we see the chaos they were feeling. Success had left them stranded, creatively, the same way that U2 were before they pulled themselves together to go in a new direction and make “Achtung Baby!” We also see how testy and difficult Townshend could be. That can happen when you’re the leader who doesn’t know where to lead. Watching this footage, I kept wishing that someone had made a Townshend biopic 30 years ago starring the young Ralph Fiennes. 

	But, of course, the Who pulled through and found a new level of sonic triumph. I’ve often gone easy on the hagiographic side of music docs, and the reason is simple: While I prefer to get the full picture, if a movie plays down the dark side of an artist, but captures that artist’s music and career with vibrant appreciation, that can be enough to make an enlightening and captivating film. But “Behind Blue Eyes” may be a special case. The movie centers itself on Pete Townshend’s contradictions, his growing pains, his turmoil, and his complexity as a human being and rock artist. And that’s all good. But given where it sets the bar, there’s too much left out.

	We learn a great deal about Townshend’s struggle to make “Lifehouse,” an unfinished science-fiction rock opera that he became obsessed with to the point that it starts to sound like something out of “Spinal Tap.” But we learn virtually nothing about Townshend’s close relationships, notably his two marriages. In 1980, when “Rough Boys,” his first solo single, was released, Townshend gave interviews acknowledging that he had, for a time, led a gay existence. Why isn’t that in the movie? And though we hear the gritty addiction details of Townshend’s dark period (when he’d become a junkie and was, by his own description, drinking three bottles of Cognac a day), what I wanted from the documentary wasn’t a bottoming-out-and-getting-sober narrative. I wanted the movie, and Townshend himself, to go deeper into why he descended into addiction.
	

	As a rock biography, “Behind Blue Eyes” is “exploratory” yet fuzzy. It’s not as riveting a portrait of the Who as “The Kids Are Alright” was (though there’s consistently great stuff in it), and for all its confessional aura it doesn’t leave you feeling that you truly know and understand Pete Townshend. It’s more like you’ve glimpsed him around the edges, without quite touching the bad man, or the sad man, behind blue eyes.

title: Andrew Scott Has Waited His Whole Career for a Role Like ‘Elsinore.’ Can Focus and the Bard Anoint Him With an Oscar?
description:
Andrew Scott is the prince of Telluride.

	There are performances that feel like a reckoning, and performances that feel like a resurrection. Andrew
body:
Andrew Scott is the prince of Telluride.

	There are performances that feel like a reckoning, and performances that feel like a resurrection. Andrew Scott’s work in “Elsinore,” which had its world premiere Friday night at the Telluride Film Festival, is somehow both — a great actor playing a great actor as the curtain starts to fall, and refusing to let it.

	Directed by Simon Stone and written by Stephen Beresford, “Elsinore” tells the true story of Ian Charleson, the Scottish “Chariots of Fire” star who spent the last year of his life playing Hamlet at London’s National Theatre as AIDS was quietly taking his life. He died in 1990 at 40. His Hamlet — hailed then as one of the finest of its generation — became a farewell disguised as a role. 
	

	The casting is too perfect to be accidental. Scott is himself a celebrated London Hamlet, here playing a man whose Hamlet was his last act of defiance. “Elsinore” is, at its heart, a love letter to actors — to the craft as vocation, to the courage of standing in the light when the body is failing. And a milestone waits inside the role. No openly gay man has ever won the Oscar for best actor, and Scott could very well become the first.


	Make no mistake, this is the role of Scott’s career and it lands him toward the forefront of a best actor conversation he has been circling for years. He has never been Oscar-nominated — a fact that curdled into open disdain when the Academy passed over his shattering turn in “All of Us Strangers.” “Elsinore” is the correction: he captures Charleson’s wit, vanity, terror and grace inside the same breath and in the final stretch, he nails Hamlet’s readiness measured against a dying man’s own — the sustained high-wire work voters still see behind their eyes in January.
	

	It’s also a role the Academy has never resisted. Voters are reliably moved by the actor staring down the barrel of death — Tom Hanks in “Philadelphia” (1993), Matthew McConaughey in “Dallas Buyers Club” (2013) and Anthony Hopkins vanishing into dementia in “The Father” (2020).



	

					Andrew Scott in “Elsinore”
									Courtesy of LFF
	



	“Elsinore” hands Scott the AIDS-era variation, with the added charge of real history — a story to discover even for those who think they already know it. Charleson was a real man and a real actor, dying as he did, playing Hamlet as he did. That is not a fact that asks for votes so much as one that issues a commandment, and I dare any Academy member not to see the worth in honoring such a life through a vessel as gifted as Scott.

	Then there is Olivia Colman, who has entered her “Maggie Smith” era and is plainly having the time of her life. Her supporting turn as Charleson’s doctor is all steel and mischief — grumpy one moment, gutting the next — the work of a past winner (“The Favourite”) who keeps finding registers no one knew she had. It belongs in the supporting actress conversation without an asterisk, the season’s most quotable grande dame showcase since Smith herself. Watch, too, for Billie Piper, as a casting director and Charleson’s confidant, who does the quietest and maybe the most surprising work in the film. It’s a stealth turn. Stone directed her to an Olivier Award in his radical stage “Yerma,” and their reunion could carry her into a film-awards conversation for the first time. If Focus campaigns her with nerve, she’s a supporting actress spoiler nobody is clocking just yet.

	The rest of the craft work is impeccable. Stefan Gregory’s score rips — propulsive where you brace for a sonorous monologue, tender where you expect something loud. Stone directs with a theater maker’s reverence for the actor’s face; Beresford, who wrote “Pride,” has built a script funnier than any logline would suggest and gutting exactly when it must be. One curious wrinkle: the script credit reads “based on an idea by Ethan Silverman,” which raises the kind of question pundits love — a “Barbie”-style scramble over whether the Academy files it as original or adapted. The WGA has designated it original.
	

	What ultimately matters is this: is it Scott only, or should we brace for more?

	A lead performance, fully embraced, can drag a whole film up the ballot. Sandra Bullock’s “The Blind Side” was beloved enough to pull the movie into best picture — its only other nomination — and she won. “Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close” managed the same trick, riding supporting actor nominee Max von Sydow to a best picture berth; it won neither, but von Sydow was plainly the runner-up to Christopher Plummer’s winning turn in “Beginners” — itself that film’s only nomination.

	Then there are the critically adored turns that stand alone. Colin Firth in Tom Ford’s “A Single Man” managed exactly one nomination — his — and lost. A year later, folded inside the 12-nomination embrace of “The King’s Speech,” he walked away with the prize. A lone acting nod is a precarious perch, and Scott will need more than that to convert his into a trophy. “Elsinore” likely needs Colman and Piper in supporting, Beresford’s screenplay on the ballot — or perhaps techs like makeup and editing — and even a best picture berth. A great performance gets you nominated; a film full of them gets you onstage.

	This can be Focus Features’ specialty. No specialty distributor has been better over the last 25 years at minting best actor winners from biopics — Adrien Brody (“The Pianist”), Sean Penn (“Milk”), Matthew McConaughey (“Dallas Buyers Club”), Eddie Redmayne (“The Theory of Everything”) and Gary Oldman (“Darkest Hour”) — five men, each playing a real one, each launched off a fall-festival bow and a patient platform release. And every one of those films was a best picture nominee.

	“Elsinore” follows the blueprint to the letter.

	The material carries its own Oscar pedigree — and Focus is riding it. Last winter the studio won its first best actress Oscar with Jessie Buckley in “Hamnet,” the story of the family loss that gave the world “Hamlet”; a few years earlier, Kenneth Branagh, cinema’s foremost Shakespearean, took original screenplay for the Focus release “Belfast.” The Academy’s affection reaches back further, to the wins “Shakespeare in Love” minted for Gwyneth Paltrow and Judi Dench. Now, two years running, the studio has a “Hamlet” in the race. The Bard has been good to this address.
	

	Hamlet’s final words are “the rest is silence.” “Elsinore,” and the actor at its center, make a beautiful liar of the line. On Friday night in the mountains, the rest was a room on its feet and an actor, at last, getting the reception for the role he was born to play.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
                          I Hope My Fertility Journey Can Educate Others

                              September 5, 2026
                            5:45 PM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says her fertility journey isn't just about her ... it's also about being a resource for women going through the same struggle.
      
    
            Our TMZ DC reporter Charlie Cotton recently caught up with the congresswoman from New York ... and asked how freezing her eggs is going.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            She told us it's going well ... saying she's happy with the results so far in the process.
      

            Charlie asked her why she chose to share this deeply personal moment of her life ... and she says it's because she couldn't find many women sharing their stories when she looked -- and she wants to be a resource for other people moving forward.
      
    
            She says the more people talk about it -- and normalize discussing it -- the easier it will be for people on a personal and professional level.
      
    
            As for how many kids she wants ... ya gotta listen to the clip all the way through -- sounds like AOC's still making up her mind.
      
    
            Of course, don't necessarily expect the rep. to have kids anytime soon ... she's not currently in a relationship -- and she says she'd like to have kids in a partnership, though that doesn't sound like a dealbreaker.
      
    
            Ultimately, AOC's going to trust the process ... and keep people informed on social media!

title: Ex-'Wheel' Announcer Jim Thornton: Photo Shows 'Panic' After Airline Discovers Pedophile Chat
body:
Ex-"Wheel of Fortune" announcer Jim Thornton worried someone saw him in an online chat for pedophiles ... at least according to a photo taken moments after a flight attendant confronted him.
      
    
            TMZ obtained the pic taken back in May by a passenger seated near Thornton on an American Airlines flight. The passenger grew concerned after seeing chatroom messages on Thornton's laptop about "cute boys" and a "hot little girl" at a restaurant ... so she reported it to a flight attendant.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In the new photo, Jim is on his phone reading the results of a Google A.I. search shortly after the flight attendant -- who'd spoken to the concerned passenger -- forced him to close his laptop.
      

            The question he asked the A.I. search is unclear, but what we can see of the screen reads, “No link to your room: Unless you explicitly told someone ... 'I am hosting this specific chatroom on for right now 'nobody [illegible] at your internet [illegible] … and link your …. identity to the … [illegible] room.”
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Another line on his screen, which is mostly covered by Thornton’s hand, reads, “Why you … [illegible] to Panic. Even if some …”
      
    
            The passenger tells us Thornton seemed nervous after the FA made him shut down his laptop.
      
    
            TMZ broke the story ... multiple photos show Thornton engaged with others in Lifeline.chat, some of whom told him it was risky to be in the chat while on a commercial flight. He boasted no one around him would be able to tell.
      
    
            Using the handle "NicholasB77," Thornton said, "What if someone sees a random sequence of lines on a screen. I love it. I hide the part that says "Lifeline" so it's just a few lines. It's a big middle finger to da man who takes away every other enjoyable activity."
      
    
            He also named a different pedophile site and claimed he was going to go there to "start looking at the galleries! Heheeeeee.” 
      
    
            As we reported ... the flight attendant told the captain about Thornton's messages, and the captain told law enforcement to greet them at the gate at LAX. 
      
    
            Jim’s lawyer told TMZ ... her client had “become active in suicide-prevention advocacy” since he lost a family member to suicide, so he frequently visits 988lifeline.org.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Thornton claims someone from that group sent him the link to lifeline.chat -- the one for pedos -- and left the website immediately after finding out it wasn’t the suicide prevention chat. However, the photos -- which show time stamps in the chat -- show Jim was in there for nearly an hour.
      
    
            Thornton’s lawyer pointed out it's “not unlawful” to be in that chat, there was no child pornography shared ... and her client was not arrested or charged with a crime after law enforcement questioned him at LAX.
      
    
            TMZ was first to report ... Thornton is now fired from "Wheel of Fortune," following Sony Pictures Television Studio conducting its own investigation.
      
    
            We reached out to Thornton's attorney for comment about his AI search, but they had no comment.
      
    
            If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.
